newsitem.title: UK: Turkey's Eurobond awaits better sentiment -bankers.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Eurobond awaits better sentiment -bankers.

text.p: Political turmoil and credit downgrades have muddied Turkey's borrowing prospects, and the country's government is prepared to keep its next Eurobond issue on hold for as long as takes for sentiment to improve, bankers said on Thursday.
Turkey was expected to issue a $250 million five-year Eurobond around mid-April, but the government postponed the deal, citing volatility in the U.S. Treasury market.
"There's always a price where a deal can get done, but Turkey isn't desperate and I don't think you'll see them chasing the market," said one banker.
The government is unlikely to launch the issue until it believes it can raise the funds at a 75 to 80 basis point pickup over its existing dollar debt, bankers familiar with the deal said.
The spread on Turkey's dollar bond maturing in 1999 is in the low 200s b.p., and Turkey was targeting a spread in the high 200s b.p. on the planned five-year Eurobond issue, bankers said.
Turkey already held roadshows in key financial centres in Europe, Asia and the United States in April. JP Morgan and SBC Warburg were appointed to underwrite the deal.

But investor appetite for emerging market instruments has languished ever since the U.S. Federal Reserve tightened credit in late March. The Fed's next policy meeting is on May 20, and many economists believe it is poised to lift interest rates further.
The Philippines and Hungary, amongst others, have also delayed their Eurodollar issue plans because of weak market conditions.
"Turkey's problems are two-fold," said another banker. "The (Treasury) market has been tricky for new issues and political unrest has put the (Eurobond) issue on a firm hold."
Turkey, which services around $7.5 billion of external debt annually, has said it planned to raise at least $2.0 billion from international capital markets this year.
Bankers agreed that Turkey's borrowing agenda may be too aggressive to achieve this year unless the political crisis cools soon.
Conflicts between Turkey's Islamist-led government and the military over the role of Islam in public life have loomed as the country moves to draw up plans to stabilise its economy.
Political turbulence has raised the country's borrowing costs and complicated Turkey's efforts to decide on a medium-term programme to tackle run-away inflation.
And economists worry that any economic programme, which must win approval from the IMF, would be difficult to implement in the midst of a political crisis.
Yet a survey conducted by Merrill Lynch showed that volatility in the U.S. Treasury market was more important to emerging fixed income investors than country risk.
International credit rating agencies recently cut Turkey's debt rating. The country has a B rating from Standard and Poor's and B1 from Moody's.

Turkey had issued 300 billion lira of five-year and 500 million marks of seven year Eurobonds earlier this year, taking advantage of favourable market conditions despite its speculative credit ratings from leading agencies.
